activities.anchor: the master's name carried the work's value
activities.caption: pair each object with its honest attribution wording
activities.name: acfAttributionMatch

config.prompt: The field's graded wording exists for a reason — pair the object with its honest formula:

pairs.left: a marble version of a lost Greek bronze, in a Roman villa
pairs.right: a Roman copy of a Greek original

pairs.left: temple or tomb production finished by apprentices
Koons's stainless-steel balloon dogs, Hirst's formaldehyde animals
pairs.right: executed by others, signed by the artist

pairs.left: the certificate accompanying a contemporary edition
'is this a Praxiteles?' about a villa marble
pairs.right: often malformed — date and place the copy instead

config.why: Authorship was structurally distributed — in antiquity by workshop, today by design — so the honest answers are formulas, not verdicts.

activities.anchor: existed for the god, not the connoisseur
activities.caption: file the purposes — what was the object for?
activities.name: acfPurposeBuckets

config.prompt: Before judging an object, reconstruct what it was for. File each fact:

items.label: a Greek cult statue's value is ritual efficacy
painted brightly, meant to be seen at festival scale
a Roman villa copy as a badge of Greek paideia
accuracy mattered less than the type
the museum's accession file as the object's biography

config.why: Forgeries exploit the purpose's expectations (a 'lost Vermeer' for a market hungry for Vermeer); conservators are bound by it — the altarpiece must keep working as an altarpiece.

config.prompt: Two heavy cases and one century of paperwork — put the dates in order:
items: the Elgin Marbles removed from the Parthenon (1801–12)
the British government purchases the Marbles (1816)
the Benin Bronzes looted in the punitive expedition (1897)
the Washington Principles commit institutions to identifying looted works (1998)
German institutions formally transfer Benin ownership to Nigeria (2022)
config.why: Provenance research is source criticism — acquisition registers, export licences, shipping manifests — applied where the stakes are legal restitution and eight-figure prices.

activities.anchor: means the object is fake or looted
activities.caption: true or false — reading the gaps
activities.name: acfGapJudge

statements.s: A provenance gap means the object is fake or looted.
statements.why: Gaps are the norm for old objects — private sales rarely generated paper before the modern era; what matters is the pattern.

statements.s: Documents consistent with known dealers and exhibitions make a good pattern.
statements.why: Documents that surface conveniently with new ink make the bad one.

statements.s: Reputable attribution opinions are stamped 'genuine' or 'fake'.
statements.why: They are worded — 'attributed to', 'workshop of', 'circle of' — because the tribunal is probabilistic.

statements.s: Attribution and provenance are probabilistic: the tribunal weighs convergent evidence and states its confidence.
statements.why: That is exactly why the graded wording exists.

activities.anchor: dates the last firing of ceramics
activities.caption: pin the pigment on the instrument's clock
activities.name: acfPrussianPlace

config.prompt: Prussian blue enters painters' palettes — around when?
config.why: 1704 — so Prussian blue cannot appear in a genuine pre-1704 painting. Anachronism is proof of forgery; but authenticity of every pigment proves only the materials, not the hand.
config.context: Titanium white enters commerce around 1921; thermoluminescence dates a ceramic's last firing — the clock that exposed forged Etruscan terracottas.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the instrument panel's limits
activities.name: acfScienceSpot

config.prompt: This technical report contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: X-radiography reveals density: paintings under paintings, and pentimenti — a changed hand position argues for an original.
Infrared reflectography maps carbon-based underdrawing beneath the paint.
Pigment analysis: titanium white (a 20th-century pigment) cannot be in a genuine Rembrandt.
Every pigment in the painting tests period-correct, so the hand is certified authentic.
Instruments bound the possible; the human tribunal judges within those bounds.
config.correction: Correct materials prove only the materials — old canvases and historically accurate pigments are purchasable; no instrument certifies a hand.
config.why: Van Meegeren used period canvases and lapis-based blues and fooled the 1937 eye; his exposure came from chemistry (phenol-formaldehyde resin) and confession, not from any instrument the experts had.

activities.caption: chair the committee — three ways to receive a 'lost Vermeer'
activities.name: acfForgeryBranch

config.root: You chair an attribution committee. A 'lost Vermeer' appears — painted in the religious middle period one leading scholar has hypothesised and longed for.

start.text: Where does the committee look first?

choices.label: Trust the leading scholar's eye — he predicted this period
Ask the simplest documentary questions first
choices.feedback: The question nobody asked at Knoedler.

choices.label: Send it to the instrument panel and wait
choices.feedback: Necessary — but it bounds, it does not certify.

hero.text: The forgery flatters expectation: van Meegeren painted the Vermeer the experts wanted, and Bredius hailed The Supper at Emmaus in print. Expectation is the vulnerability.

docs.text: Coherence is not evidence: the Knoedler fraud sold roughly $80M of fakes from one undocumented 'estate' because the story was good, the desire strong, and nobody asked the simplest documentary questions.

panel.text: Instruments bound the possible — period canvas and hand-ground pigments pass every chronological test. Van Meegeren was exposed by chemistry he could not hide (phenol-formaldehyde resin, detectable 1945) and by confession.

config.why: The defence is institutional — independent committees, published provenance, instrument panels — because the vulnerability is psychological, not optical.

activities.caption: drag the divider — the Sistine ceiling, before and after
activities.name: acfSistineCompare

config.prompt: The standard seminar on interpretation-as-cleaning — drag between the two states:

before.label: Before 1980
before.text: Grime and darkening lacquinature glazes — the Michelangelo of candle smoke; the colours everyone thought they knew.

after.label: After the 1980–94 cleaning
after.text: The astonishing colours return — and the Beck–Vatican controversy erupts: were the a secco glazes original finishing layers or later dirt?

config.why: Every cleaning decision is a theory of what the object was — minimum intervention, reversibility, distinct retouching, full documentation; future generations outrank present audiences.
